fixes.answer: The effects can be genuinely serious. Prolonged loneliness is strongly linked to mental health problems such as depression and anxiety. It can also have physical consequences, as chronic isolation is thought to weaken the immune system and even affect [[longevity]]. Beyond that, it can trap people in a negative cycle, where low mood makes them [[withdraw]] further, deepening the isolation and their sense of [[despair]].
fixes.why: 'isolation' is the topic word and plain; marked 'longevity'

fixes.answer: I fear it might, if current trends continue. As societies become more individualistic and people increasingly work and socialise remotely, opportunities for spontaneous human contact may [[diminish]]. An ageing population in many countries could also worsen the situation. However, I remain hopeful that growing awareness of the issue will [[prompt]] communities and governments to take [[preventive]] action.

Communities can play a powerful role. Creating accessible public spaces and organising local events, from community gardens to social clubs, gives people natural opportunities to connect. Initiatives that specifically reach out to isolated individuals, like [[befriending schemes]] for the elderly, are especially valuable. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a culture where people look out for their neighbours can rebuild the [[social fabric]] that has frayed.
fixes.why: 'isolated' is plain; marked 'befriending schemes' and the full phrase 'social fabric'

fixes.answer: Certainly not; there is an important distinction between loneliness and healthy [[solitude]]. Chosen time alone can be genuinely [[restorative]], allowing for reflection, creativity and rest. Many people find solitude essential for recharging. The problem arises only when isolation is [[involuntary]] and prolonged. So spending time alone is perfectly healthy, as long as it is balanced with meaningful connection.
